entries.q: We should judge things as they are, not as they are reported.
entries.b: Seneca noticed that a rumor passes through a hundred mouths before it reaches the ear, and each mouth seasons it. Your own mind does the same thing with events: the neutral report arrives, and by the time you react, three retellings have exaggerated it. The curt message becomes hostility. The delayed reply becomes contempt. Today, hear the raw report first: what literally happened, in words a camera would agree with. The courtroom in your head should demand evidence before verdicts, like any decent court.
entries.x: Take one judgment you made today and state only the camera-verifiable facts.

entries.q: Accustom yourself to believe that death is nothing to us, and judge every portrait of disaster before you hang it.
entries.b: Seneca advised his friend Lucilius to pre-judge the stories he would hear each day, because a mind that expects distortions cannot be ruled by them. Every day you hang portraits in your inner gallery: the boss disapproves of me, the friend is drifting away, the stranger meant that insult. Before hanging any of them, look closely. Half are painted by insecurity, a quarter by tiredness, the rest by genuine information you could simply ask about. Curate the gallery. Walls get crowded fast.
entries.x: Ask one direct question today instead of accepting a painted portrait.

entries.q: The happiness of your life depends upon the quality of your thoughts.
entries.b: Two people sit in the same meeting and leave with different days. One heard a criticism and spent the afternoon defending himself internally. The other heard information and spent the afternoon improving the work. The meeting was identical; the dial settings differed. Marcus believed the mind has dials, interpretation settings, that most of us never touch because we were handed them preset by parents, culture, and old wounds. Today is a good day to walk over to the dial and adjust one deliberately.
entries.x: Notice your default interpretation setting on one event. Try a different setting on purpose.

entries.q: Do not pronounce sentence before the trial.
entries.b: Epictetus told his students that most people convict on rumor, on a facial expression, on a feeling in the stomach. The spouse who seems distant is convicted of indifference. The manager who says we need to talk is convicted of firing you. The trials in real life are short and survivable; the pre-trials in imagination are long and ruinous. Suspend the verdict. Let evidence arrive. You will be surprised how often the accused walks free, and how much calmer the courtroom is in the meantime.
entries.x: Refuse one premature verdict today. Wait for the actual conversation.

entries.q: Everything is opinion, and opinion is in our power.
entries.b: You look at your life through a window, but you rarely notice the frame. Too narrow and everything seems like lack; too ornate and everything seems like drama. A coworker's promotion, framed as theft, poisons the office. Framed as information about what works here, it improves your own path. Epictetus claimed the frame, not the view, is the real possession. Other people's frames are pressed against the glass constantly, offering you theirs: jealous, resentful, fearful. You are permitted to decline the loan.
entries.x: Reframe one situation today in a frame that makes action possible.

entries.q: Take away the opinion, and there is taken away the complaint: I have been harmed.
entries.b: A comment is made. A hundred people might hear it, but only you amplify it, and the volume you choose determines the injury. Marcus treated opinion as an amplifier: turn it up and a pebble becomes an avalanche, turn it down and even real harm becomes survivable. This is not about denial. Real harm exists and deserves response. But most of what echoes in your head today was a pebble, and you are the one running the sound board. Check the levels.
entries.x: Turn down one amplified grievance today to its original volume.

entries.q: How much more grievous are the consequences of anger than the causes of it.
entries.b: The cause of your anger this morning may have occupied three seconds. The anger itself: the clenched hour, the sharp reply, the story retold to three friends, the mood your children absorbed. Marcus noticed anger's arithmetic is catastrophic; consequences dwarf causes a hundred to one. The stranger who cut you off spent nothing. You have been paying ever since. When someone hands you their garbage, the tragedy would be carrying it home. Leave it where it was dropped.
entries.x: When anger arrives today, ask what it will cost you by evening. Then decide.

entries.q: Be silent for the most part, or say only what is necessary, and judge little.
entries.b: Epictetus noticed that judgment and speech travel together: the more we narrate other people's flaws aloud, the more our minds rehearse the judging. The lunch complaint, the group chat analysis, the running commentary on strangers. Each retelling deepens the grooves. This is not a rule about being pleasant. It is an observation about attention: every spoken judgment is a repetition, and repetition is how the mind learns what to look for. Speak less of others' failings and your eyes begin to find something else.
entries.x: Go one conversation today without judging anyone absent. Notice the pull.

entries.q: First tell yourself what kind of world this is, and what kind of people inhabit it.
entries.b: Marcus expected the office politics, the selfishness, the vanity, and so was never disillusioned. We, expecting none of it, are disillusioned daily. The first story we tell is that people should be better than this. The second story, the Stoic one, is that people are exactly what training and temperament have made them, and our job is to remain good anyway. Neither story changes the world. But the first one leaves you betrayed every morning. The second leaves you free to work.
entries.x: Rewrite one disappointment today using the second story: people are people, and I remain good anyway.

entries.q: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views they take of them. Death is nothing to us, but the view of death is terrifying.
entries.b: Epictetus pointed out that your most stressful opinions were not chosen. They were inherited: money means security, success means worth, being disliked means danger. You picked them up before you could read. This is not an accusation, it is an opening. Inherited opinions can be examined like any other furniture, and some of it can be sold. The opinion that every email needs an instant reply, that rest must be earned, that other people's success is your loss. Check the provenance. You may be living in someone else's house.
entries.x: Examine one inherited belief today. Ask who installed it and whether it still serves.

entries.q: Choose not to react at the speed of the provocation.
entries.b: The mind wants to answer insult within seconds, and the answer drafted in the first seconds is almost always the worst available. Marcus, who received genuine insults from senators, practiced a delay: the gap between provocation and reply is where your character gets to vote. In your life the stakes are similar even when smaller. The message written in anger, the decision made in a flush of feeling. Draft nothing permanent in the first minute. The second minute knows things the first does not.
entries.x: Delay one reply today by an hour. Read it again before sending.

entries.q: Ascend above the narrow frame and look down on the crowds, the harvests, the marriages, the lawsuits.
entries.b: From high enough, Marcus said, you can see the whole human comedy: the arguments that consume mornings, the ambitions that consume decades, all of them brief and strangely similar. This is not an invitation to sneer. It is medicine for the person drowning in their own drama. From the wide frame, the disagreement with your neighbor looks like what it is. But notice the other half: from the wide frame, your loved ones look infinitely precious too. Zoom out for size, then zoom back in for love.
entries.x: Spend one minute today looking at your life from the wide frame.

entries.q: Complaining adds nothing. Subtract nothing. Change nothing, except the complainer.
entries.b: Track a typical complaint to its end and see what it purchased: a small hit of agreement, a temporary alliance against the world, and a deeper groove of resentment. The weather did not improve, the coworker did not reform, the queue did not shorten. The Stoics were not against naming problems; they were against the performed grievance that feels like action and replaces it. Today, convert every complaint into either a request, an action, or a release. Those are the only three honorable destinations.
entries.x: Convert one complaint today into a request, an action, or a release.

entries.q: Do not follow the common sort in judging by appearance, nor the crowd in assuming.
entries.b: Every assumption is a loan the mind takes out against reality. He ignored me, so he is angry. She got the role, so politics. The debt comes due as behavior: you act cold toward someone who was merely busy, you sour on an opportunity that was merely hard. Marcus, ruling millions of people he would never meet, knew how expensive borrowed conclusions are. Today, mark every assumption as you make it. Where you can, repay in cash: ask, observe, or wait.
entries.x: Catch one assumption today and convert it into a question.

entries.q: First, do not be agitated: everything happens according to the nature of the whole. Second, the offender was doing what seemed right to him.
entries.b: Marcus's protocol for offense has two steps, and both buy time. Step one: the world was never going to be smooth, so nothing is out of order. Step two: the person who wronged you acted on what seemed right to them, from their level of sight, just as you once acted from yours. This does not excuse them. It recalibrates you. From there, the options widen past rage: correct them, avoid them, tolerate them, or let it go. All four are still on the table when you are calm.
entries.x: Apply the two steps to one offense today before responding.

entries.q: Everything we hear is an opinion, not a fact.
entries.b: A single sentence lands differently in every ear that hears it. The feedback was neutral; the reader added the sting. The compliment was sincere; the reader discounted it as politeness. Marcus understood that we are not consumers of events but co-authors, and the authorship is invisible because it happens so fast. Slow the moment down once today. Find the exact point where the neutral words became your feelings. That point is not the world's. It is yours, and it can be edited.
entries.x: Find one place today where you added the sting to neutral words.

entries.q: The best revenge is not to be like your enemy.
entries.b: Something happened years ago that you still carry, a wrong whose heat survives in memory. Marcus's insight is that the wrong finished long ago; the carrying is what continues, and the carrying changes you into its shape. To be like your enemy is not to imitate their cruelty. It is to let their single act keep acting through you, years past the scene. Put down what can be put down. Not for them. For the shape you are becoming, which deserves better material.
entries.x: Set down one old wrong for one day. Notice the shape of your hours without it.

entries.q: Whenever you are about to judge someone, imagine their whole life laid before you.
entries.b: The colleague who snapped at you: carrying what you cannot see? The slow cashier: on hour nine of a double shift? Marcus asked for the whole biography before the verdict, knowing we usually judge a single frame. The driver who swerved, the relative who cancelled, the friend who forgot. A whole life is a heavy thing to weigh in three seconds, and honest judges admit it. Today, when judgment rises, give the accused the courtesy of a longer story. You would want the same.
entries.x: Give one person today the courtesy of a longer story before judging.

entries.q: It never ceases to amaze me: we all love ourselves more than other people, but we care more about their opinion than our own.
entries.b: You know yourself: the intentions, the effort, the reasons. Strangers know a sliver, and yet their sliver outweighs your whole library in your own valuation. Marcus found this absurd, and it is. The crowd whose approval you court this week could not describe your last good day. Meanwhile the one judge who has seen everything, you, is overruled constantly. Weight the testimony properly. Not with arrogance, with accuracy: their view is a weather report from far away.
entries.x: Let one outside opinion carry less weight today than your own knowledge of yourself.

entries.q: The soul is dyed by the color of its judgments.
entries.b: The mind runs a label machine: lazy, difficult, rude, hopeless. Stick a label on someone and perception stops; the label does the seeing. Your difficult coworker had a name before they had a label, and a childhood before they had a name. The Stoic move is not saintly patience. It is accuracy: labels are lossy, they compress a person to a word, and decisions made on compressed data are usually bad ones. Remove one label today and look at what was underneath.
entries.x: Remove one label today. Look at the person or situation plainly for five minutes.

entries.q: Between the event and the response there is a space, and in that space is your freedom.
entries.b: The provocation lands and the mind offers two reflexes: attack or absorb. The Stoics insisted there is always a third option, and usually a fourth, fifth, and sixth, visible only in the pause. The awkward silence after the insult is not weakness; it is a workshop. In it, you can ask: what does this moment actually call for? Sometimes nothing. Sometimes humor. Sometimes one firm sentence. The reflex chooses fast and badly. The pause chooses slowly and well.
entries.x: Take one full breath before responding to anything that provokes you today.

entries.q: How much time he gains who does not look to see what his neighbour says or does.
entries.b: Most of us run a second, invisible job: monitoring the imaginary audience. How did that land? What will they think? The audience is largely fictional, half-distracted, and thinking about themselves. Marcus calculated the hours recovered by a mind that stops performing. It is not that others' views never matter; reputation has uses. It is that the imagined tribunal convenes dozens of times a day and issues verdicts nobody cares about. Adjourn the court. The recovered hours are yours to spend on actual work and actual people.
entries.x: Catch yourself performing for the imaginary audience once today. Stop, and return to the task.

entries.q: Judge a thing by what it is, and your day by what it was, not by what it should have been.
entries.b: Epictetus drew a line between the event and the expectation, and noticed we grieve the expectation more than the event. The weekend was rained out: the event was rain, the expectation was sunshine, and the suffering lived in the gap. Practicing this daily is not lowering your standards. It is living on the actual ground instead of the imagined one. The day that was is always knowable and usually usable. The day that should have been is a ghost that eats real hours.
entries.x: Accept one today for what it was, not what it should have been.

entries.q: When angry, ask: what opinion of mine was just struck?
entries.b: Seneca taught that anger is almost always a secondary emotion: beneath it sits a struck belief. The rudeness stings because you believe you deserve courtesy. The criticism burns because you believe you are competent. The belief may be entirely sound; the anger is still just its alarm. Find the belief and the anger becomes navigable, because beliefs can be examined and defended, while raw anger can only be discharged, usually at the wrong target. Ask what was struck. Then decide whether the belief needs defense or adjustment.
entries.x: Find the belief behind one moment of anger today.

entries.q: Loss is nothing else but change, and change is Nature's delight.
entries.b: The mind resists change as though it were an attack, when it is the oldest and most reliable policy of the universe. Your job changed, your child grew up, your city moved on. Marcus recommended meeting change the way you meet seasons: with preparation, some grief, and eventual participation. The judgment that change is loss is optional. The judgment that it is the world's ongoing work is accurate. Grieve what deserves grief. Then notice you are being asked to grow into the new arrangement, not merely endure it.
entries.x: Name one change you have resisted. Find one thing it is asking you to become.

entries.q: It is a shame for the soul to be troubled by another's fault, which is theirs, not yours.
entries.b: Read the fine print on most offense: you have taken responsibility for another adult's character. Their rudeness becomes your bad afternoon. Their dishonesty becomes your vigilance and your ranting. Marcus found the accounting backwards; their faults are their ledger entries, heavy on their side, and you have somehow volunteered to carry them. Hand the weight back. Address what needs addressing, protect what needs protecting, and leave their character where it lives: with them.
entries.x: Hand back one responsibility for another person's character today.

entries.q: If anyone tells you that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make excuses about what is said. Answer: he does not know the rest of my faults.
entries.b: This is Epictetus's most disarming move. Defensiveness assumes the critic is wrong and must be corrected. The trained mind assumes the critic has, at best, seen a fraction, and the fraction may even be right. The strange freedom in this: if you already know your faults better than any gossip, criticism loses its power to shock. It becomes one more voice describing what you are already working on. Security about your flaws is the strongest armor there is.
entries.x: When criticism arrives today, look for the part that is true first.

entries.q: The mind adapts and converts to its own purposes the obstacle to our acting.
entries.b: Look back on a year that went wrong, and then look again for what it forced into existence: the skill built, the relationship deepened, the move you would never have chosen. The events did not change. The judgment about them did, given time and evidence. Marcus proposed borrowing that hindsight early: treat this year's obstacle now the way you will treat it in five years, as material. You cannot rewrite the event. You are always free to write early the interpretation you would eventually have written late.
entries.x: Apply five-year hindsight to one current obstacle today.

entries.q: The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing; but the judging mind can rest.
entries.b: A month of watching your own judgments reveals the machinery: how fast the labels form, how often the assumption is wrong, how much of your weather was self-authored. The reward is not a mind that judges nothing; judgment is necessary for living. The reward is a mind that knows it is judging, and therefore judges slowly, fairly, and lightly. Clear sight is not a talent. It is a practice, and you have now practiced it for four weeks. Keep the glasses clean.
entries.x: Write down one thing you judged too quickly this month. Forgive the judging; keep the lesson.
